meta.title: Who really said "Each time you fail, start all over again, and you will grow stronger until you find that you have accomplished a purpose"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Helen Keller. She wrote it down in her 1955 book Teacher — crediting the words to her own teacher, Anne Sullivan. Chapter 12, page 156.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Each time you fail, start all over again, and you will grow stronger until you find that you have accomplished a purpose'?
meta.ogDescription: Keller recorded it; Anne Sullivan said it. Sourced to Teacher: Anne Sullivan Macy (Doubleday, 1955), ch. 12, p. 156, verified by Quote Investigator.

answer.label: Not Helen Keller — actually Anne Sullivan
answer.authorDates: 1866–1936 · teacher and lifelong companion of Helen Keller
answer.sourceLine: Helen Keller did write the sentence down — but she wrote it down as her teacher’s. It appears in Keller’s 1955 tribute Teacher: Anne Sullivan Macy, chapter 12, page 156, where Keller credits the counsel to Anne Sullivan, the woman who taught her. Quote Investigator verified that page with scans ↗ and located no earlier appearance anywhere.

source.excerpt: No matter what happens, keep on beginning and failing. Each time you fail, start all over again, and you will grow stronger until you find that you have accomplished a purpose—not the one you began with, perhaps, but one that you will be glad to remember.
trail: 3 March 1887 — Anne Sullivan, twenty years old and partially blind from childhood trachoma, begins teaching the deaf-blind Helen Keller. The partnership runs forty-nine years ↗.
20 October 1936 — Sullivan dies ↗. Nothing resembling this saying has been found in print during her lifetime.
1955 — Keller publishes Teacher: Anne Sullivan Macy and, in chapter 12, sets down her teacher’s advice in full. Quote Investigator verified page 156 with scans ↗ and found no earlier citation.

16 November 1969 — playwright Robert Stempin gives the words to Sullivan as stage dialogue in a Scranton newspaper column, the next citation Quote Investigator records ↗ after the book itself — already slightly re-worded.
source.excerptNote: Quote Investigator’s transcription ↗ places the passage just after Keller’s line about her teacher — “And who shall count the innumerable times that she tried, failed, and conquered?” The counsel is Sullivan’s; the book carrying it is Keller’s.

author.name: Anne Sullivan
author.kicker: The woman who actually said it
author.heading: The teacher, not the pupil
author.metaLine: 1866–1936 · American teacher; Helen Keller’s instructor and companion for 49 years
author.bio: Anne Sullivan (born Johanna Mansfield Sullivan, later Anne Sullivan Macy) contracted trachoma at five and grew up partially blind, working her way through the Perkins School for the Blind and graduating as valedictorian at twenty. Weeks later she was hired to teach a deaf-blind six-year-old in Alabama, and on 3 March 1887 she began the finger-spelling method that would make Helen Keller literate — 575 words and basic Braille inside six months. The partnership ran forty-nine years, through Radcliffe and onto the public stage, but Sullivan published no memoir of her own: almost everything she is quoted as saying survives because Keller wrote it down.

Often credited to Keller herself; she was the one who wrote it down, not the one who said it.

misattribution.heading: Who gets the credit, and who earned it
misattribution.intro: This is not a fabricated quote — it is a real sentence on a findable page. What goes wrong is the name attached to it, and, in most reprints, one small missing phrase.

items.scope: The credit this page was asked about
items.why: Keller is the famous name on the only book the line has ever been found in, so the sentence gets pinned on her. Inside that book she is explicitly quoting someone else. Quote Investigator weighed exactly this confusion, heading its investigation with the candidates “Hellen Keller? Anne Sullivan? Apocryphal?” ↗ and filing the piece under Keller — before settling on Sullivan.

The aggregator layer has dropped two words. BrainyQuote’s version ↗ reads “until you have accomplished a purpose,” where Keller’s text reads “until you find that you have accomplished a purpose.” Small cut, real loss: the original is about discovering an end you did not set out for.

The quote is reproduced across motivational listicles with a name and nothing else — no book, no chapter, no year ↗. That vacuum is what lets the byline drift between teacher and pupil in the first place.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are Anne Sullivan’s, preserved by Helen Keller in Teacher: Anne Sullivan Macy (Doubleday, 1955), chapter 12, page 156 — the earliest appearance Quote Investigator could find ↗, verified against scans of the book.

context.heading: Why the wrong name sticks
lead: There is a specific way misattribution happens when a famous person writes a book about a less famous one. The sentence gets quoted, the spine gets glanced at, and the name on the cover collects the credit. Teacher: Anne Sullivan Macy is Helen Keller’s book — her prose, her copyright, her byline — and inside it she is doing the opposite of taking credit. The subtitle is “A Tribute by the Foster-child of Her Mind.” The whole point of the volume is to hand the achievement back to the teacher.

It also happens to be advice with an unusually good claim to authenticity, because Sullivan had lived it. Trachoma took most of her sight at five. She reached the Perkins School for the Blind by way of an almshouse, graduated valedictorian at twenty, and was handed a deaf-blind child she had no established method for teaching. “Keep on beginning and failing” is not a greeting-card sentiment in that mouth; it is a description of the job.
context.detailsSummary: The gap between 1936 and 1955 — and why it still holds up
detailsBody: The honest weakness in the record is timing. Sullivan died on 20 October 1936, and the words do not surface in print until Keller’s book copyrighted in 1955. Quote Investigator states the problem plainly rather than papering over it: Sullivan died in 1936, so there was a delay before Keller made this attribution — and then concludes that the evidence is nevertheless substantive. There is no contemporaneous note, no letter, no lecture transcript behind it; there is Keller’s testimony, and Keller spent forty-nine years within arm’s reach of the speaker.

The wording has also been quietly sanded down in transit. Keller’s text reads “until you find that you have accomplished a purpose” — the discovery is the point, and the sentence goes on to say the purpose will not be the one you set out with. Most reprints drop “find that,” which turns a line about being surprised by where you ended up into a flatter promise that persistence pays. The wording asked about on this page is, unusually, the accurate one.
context.pull: Keller held the pen. Sullivan supplied the sentence.
